note: Solar-storm facts for the Solar storms page (src/js/storms.js). Every number below was read from the linked NASA page or paper on 2026-11-15. Nothing here is estimated by us. Where the app combines two of these numbers, the page labels the result 'our calculation'.

events.title: First solar storm RAD saw from the ground
events.measured: Dose rate rose about 30% above the normal cosmic-ray level. The whole event added 0.025 mGy (25 μGy).
events.meaning: A small storm: Mars' thin air stopped most of it.

events.title: Radiation on the ground more than doubled
events.measured: Dose rates rose to 2 to 3 times the normal cosmic-ray level, stayed at that peak for about 12 hours, then fell over the next 36 hours. NASA: the high readings lasted more than two days. This was under 23 g/cm² of Mars air.
events.meaning: RAD's lead scientist, Don Hassler, said that someone outdoors on a Mars walk who learned such an event was coming "would definitely want to take shelter."
events.source: NASA/JPL news, 29 Sept 2017; Zeitlin et al. (2018), Geophys. Res. Lett., doi:10.1029/2018GL077760

events.title: The biggest surge RAD has measured
events.measured: After an X12 solar flare, a person standing next to Curiosity would have received 8,100 μGy, which NASA compares to 30 chest X-rays. The flare's X-rays and gamma rays arrived first; the charged particles reached Mars "in just tens of minutes."
events.meaning: Hassler: "Cliffsides or lava tubes would provide additional shielding for an astronaut from such an event."
events.source: NASA/JPL, "NASA Watches Mars Light Up During Epic Solar Storm", 10 June 2024

context.stormCount: RAD had measured more than a dozen solar storms by November 2021, five of them on the way to Mars.
context.stormCountSource: NASA/JPL, "How NASA's Curiosity Rover Is Making Mars Safer for Astronauts", 15 Nov 2021
context.cliffShielding: Parked at the foot of a cliff at Murray Buttes (9-21 Sept 2016), RAD measured 4% less radiation overall and 7.5% less neutral-particle radiation.
context.cliffSource: NASA/JPL, 15 Nov 2021; Ehresmann et al. (2021), JGR Planets, doi:10.1029/2021JE006851

health.source: NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-020 Rev E, "Design for Ionizing Radiation Protection" (27 Dec 2022)
health.duringMission: Acute radiation syndromes such as nausea, vomiting and fatigue, as well as skin injuries and depletion of blood-forming organs.
health.afterMission: A higher risk of cancer, and a risk of changes in thinking, movement and behaviour.
health.howLikely: NASA's brief says about 95% of solar particle events do not come near the dose limits, and that the chance of an EVA organ dose above 100 mSv is less than one in a million.
health.limits: NASA limits: under 250 mSv effective dose from any one solar particle event (to minimise acute effects), and under 600 mSv over a whole career.
health.unitNote: RAD reports absorbed dose (gray). NASA's limits are effective dose (sievert), which also weighs how damaging each kind of particle is. The two cannot be compared one-to-one, so this page does not convert between them.
health.evaRule: Real-time alert dosimetry gives a very high level of protection for EVAs if the EVA is ended within 2 hours and there is access to shielding.

precautions.step: Stop work and start back at once.
precautions.why: NASA: ending the EVA within 2 hours, with shielding to go to, gives a very high level of protection.

precautions.step: Do not wait to see anything.
precautions.why: In May 2024 the charged particles reached Mars tens of minutes after the flare's light. A storm cannot be seen or felt.

precautions.step: Go straight to the habitat's storm shelter.
precautions.why: NASA plans a shelter with about 10 cm of water (or similar material) added around crew quarters for a once-in-100-years storm.

precautions.step: Too far from the habitat? Put rock between you and the sky.
precautions.why: Cliffsides or lava tubes give extra shielding (Hassler, 2024). The measured gain at the foot of one cliff was small: 4% (Curiosity, 2016). It is a stop-gap, not a shelter.
NASA requires personal dose monitoring, so the crew and Earth know what each person received.

precautions.step: Stay inside until monitoring gives the all-clear.
precautions.why: In September 2017 the high readings lasted more than two days. NASA requires real-time space-weather monitoring and crew alerts.
